text: While the internet was asking chatbots how many R's are in strawberry, a different kind of AI was designing brand-new proteins from scratch.
So here's our question for today. Did AI just learn to write biology?
Because in a real lab, those proteins grabbed their targets harder than the best designs before them.
And another AI wrote a gene editor that edited human DNA in cells.
Honestly, that sounds like hype, and part of me wants to roll my eyes.
But it's all in research papers, and the field behind it has a Nobel Prize.
There's a catch too, and I promise we'll get to it.
Let's do a quick refresher first.
A protein starts as a long chain of building blocks called amino acids, and then it folds itself into a specific 3D shape.
Imagine tossing a loose string in the air and watching it land as a perfectly folded paper crane.
Real folding isn't always that neat, and when a protein folds wrong, it can make you sick.
And the shape decides the job, because it's what lets a protein grab, cut, or carry something.
Your body is basically running a nonstop origami contest, and nobody asked you to sign up.
For about fifty years, predicting that shape from the chain was one of biology's most stubborn problems.
Then an AI called AlphaFold2 solved it, and in 2024 that earned Demis Hassabis and John Jumper half of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The other half went to David Baker, for designing new proteins with computers.
Turns out a chemistry Nobel now comes with a lot of code, and somewhere a grad student pipetting at two in the morning felt that.
Here's the shift I think matters most.
Predicting a protein's shape is reading. Designing a brand-new protein for a job you picked is writing.
Reading is looking at a recipe and guessing the cake.
Writing is wanting one very specific cake and inventing a recipe nobody has written.
And if you've ever baked without a recipe, you know writing is where the smoke alarm goes off.
One big writing tool, RFdiffusion, came out of Baker's lab in a 2023 Nature paper, and it borrows the trick behind AI image generators.
Those generators start from pure static and clean it up step by step until a picture shows up.
RFdiffusion runs that same cleanup on protein shapes instead of pixels, and the lab made it open-source.
The tech behind cats in spacesuits is now sketching molecules.
Then, on September 5th, 2024, Google DeepMind announced AlphaProteo.
Which sounds like protein powder a gym influencer would sell you, but stay with me.
AlphaProteo designs binders, which are new proteins built from scratch to latch onto one specific target protein.
Think of the target as a lock, and the AI as a locksmith who cuts a brand-new key to fit it.
Stick something to a protein, and you can stop it from doing its job.
But a key on a screen is just a drawing, and the real test is whether it turns.
DeepMind made the designs and tested them in the lab.
For seven different target proteins, including a piece of the coronavirus spike, AlphaProteo produced binders that worked.
On one target, called BHRF1, eighty-eight percent of the candidates actually stuck.
Eighty-eight percent. I have never been eighty-eight percent right about anything, including where I parked.
DeepMind says its binders latched on three to three hundred times more strongly than the best existing methods.
The Francis Crick Institute then checked the results independently, and some coronavirus binders stopped the virus from infecting cells.
That's basically science for pics or it didn't happen.
That's seven targets, seven wins. And then there was target number eight.
Target eight was a protein called TNF alpha, and AlphaProteo struck out.
Every hero needs a final boss, and apparently this one's is TNF alpha.
And I'm glad they reported the miss, because it tells you this is a tool, not magic.
Okay, grabbing is cool, but editing DNA is a whole other level.
CRISPR gene editing uses two parts, a guide RNA that carries the address and a Cas protein that does the cutting.
It's basically find-and-replace for your DNA, where the guide is the search box and Cas9 is the scissors.
But after the cut, the cell does its own repairs, so it isn't always as clean as hitting replace.
It's the most powerful word processor ever made, and there is no undo button.
On April 22nd, 2024, a company called Profluent released OpenCRISPR-1, which it billed as the world's first open-source, AI-generated gene editor.
To build it, they trained a protein language model on CRISPR-Cas sequences and had it write three hundred fifty thousand new proteins.
That kind of model treats amino acids like letters and keeps guessing the next one, like the autocomplete on your phone.
But autocomplete can sound great and mean nothing, and a protein can look great and do nothing, so somebody still has to test it.
Full disclosure, AI helps make this channel too, and ours mostly suggests jokes while theirs suggests gene editors.
Profluent filtered that pile down, and the winner became OpenCRISPR-1.
Reportedly, it differs from the standard Cas9 by around four hundred amino acids and still edits about as well or better.
Evolution wrote the original code, and the AI showed up with one very large pull request.
But a pull request means nothing until it runs. So did these AI-written scissors actually edit human DNA?
They did. Profluent says it was the first time an AI-designed editor precisely edited the human genome, in human cells in a dish.
And on July 30th, 2025, the full study was published in Nature.
Peer review approved the pull request.
Here's the part I didn't see coming. Profluent made OpenCRISPR-1 free to license for ethical research and commercial use.
Some uses are off the table, like editing the human germline, meaning changes that get passed down to your kids.
So no, you can't use it to patch your future children.
And it's not just these two teams.
In June 2024, EvolutionaryScale released a model called ESM3 and used it to make a new glowing protein, esmGFP.
Its sequence matches its closest natural relative by only fifty-eight percent, and the company compared that gap to five hundred million years of evolution.
To be clear, that's a way to describe how different the sequence is, not a time machine.
Which is the most press-release way possible to say pretty different.
So far, we've got AI writing proteins that grab, cut, and glow.
Which brings us to the question everyone asks next. When does your doctor get to use any of this?
Not yet, and that's the catch I promised.
Every result in this video came from test tubes, cells, and papers, and none of it is an approved treatment.
And that creates a strange new traffic jam.
One model wrote three hundred fifty thousand candidates, but a lab still has to prove which ones actually work.
So does AI make biology faster, or does it just make the line outside the lab a lot longer?
Either way, the pipette isn't going anywhere.
Now, remember our protein powder friend, AlphaProteo?
Baker's lab open-sourced RFdiffusion, and Profluent opened up its editor, but DeepMind did not release AlphaProteo to the public.
Why keep this one locked up?
DeepMind says it chose a careful rollout instead, consulting outside experts and joining an AI and biology forum run by the Nuclear Threat Initiative.
And that points to the uncomfortable question under this whole story.
If an AI can design a protein that helps, could someone aim it at something harmful? And who checks before anything actually gets made?
The reassuring part, to me, is that scientists asked that out loud, and early.
In March 2024, more than one hundred fifty of them signed voluntary commitments on responsible AI in protein design, in an effort led in part by David Baker.
They promised things like safety reviews before releasing models, and buying synthetic DNA only from suppliers that screen orders for biosecurity.
Think of a print shop that checks every job, so nobody walks out with a stack of fake twenties.
It's voluntary, so it's less a law and more a very important group chat where everyone agreed to behave.
So, did AI learn to write biology?
I'd say kind of.
It writes drafts, some of them are shockingly good, and sometimes, like with target number eight, nothing lands.
Every one of those drafts still needed a human lab to say yes.
And hey, the Nobel still went to people, not a server rack.
Here's the thing I keep coming back to.
If a medicine designed with AI passed every human trial, would you take it? And would it matter to you who, or what, wrote it?
Personally, I care way more about the trial than the author.
Meanwhile, somewhere, a chatbot is still counting the R's in strawberry.
I'm genuinely curious, so drop your answer in the comments, and send this to the friend who keeps saying AI can't do real science.
Subscribe, and see you next meltdown.
